run_kernels.sh (the script of 2026-11-13 that built both binaries on CRB) wrote this line before the build [Ref1].
- `host`: the host name that CRB reports.
- `utc`: the start time. The folder name `kernels-20261113T181222Z` holds the same time.
- `load_before`: the load average of the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
- `logins=0`: the tool `who` listed no login session.
- `mode=all`: the script ran the build, this listing, the self-test and then the timed runs of 2026-11-13.

segments.text:
- Line 2: the first line of `gcc --version`. The compiler is gcc 14.2.0 of Ubuntu.
- Line 3: the flags of all four builds of this run [Ref1].
- `-O3`: the highest numbered optimization level of gcc.
- `-march=native`: gcc may use every instruction set of the CPU that runs the compiler. On CRB this includes SVE [Ref11].
- `-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns`: gcc must not replace a loop by a call of a library function.
- The other flags select thread support, more warnings and the C dialect.

The content of the Linux file `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` [Ref1]. The brackets mark the active setting, `always`. With `always`, Linux may back a buffer with 2 MiB pages without a request of the program (THP, see Words used here).

Line 6 is the header line of the tool `ps`. Lines 7 to 11 are the 5 processes with the highest `%CPU`, here at most 0.3 % [Ref1]. `%CPU` is an average over the life of a process. It is not the use at the moment of the reading.
The size of `build.txt`, the file that received the messages of gcc. 0 bytes means that gcc printed no warning and no error in the four builds: bw_old, bw_new, selftest and probe.o [Ref1].

- Lines 14 to 18: the four C sources and the script run_kernels.sh in the build folder. `bandwidth.orig.c` is the old source. `bandwidth.c` is the new source.
- Lines 19 and 20: the binaries bw_old and bw_new. ra.sh (the part A script of the rerun) compares both binaries with these two values before it starts a process. It stops when a value differs [Ref2].
- Line 21: the binary of the self-test.
- Line 22: the benchmark source in the folder `~/cache-perf/bench` of CRB. Its value equals line 14. So that file was the old source at the time of the build.
- The copy of `bandwidth.c` in the folder `tmp/agent-scratch/kernels-2026-11-13` of this project has another value than line 15. A later record shows that it gives the bw_new of line 20 [Ref5].

segments.text:
objdump text of the function `k_read` of bw_new. Line 24 gives its start address. Each line below holds an address (hexadecimal), an instruction name and the operands. Each instruction is 4 bytes long.
- Loop: addresses `1c64` to `1c8c` (lines 26 to 36), 11 instructions, 44 bytes of code.
- Bytes read per loop pass: 256.
- Load instructions per loop pass: 8.
- Other instructions per loop pass: 3 (`add`, `cmp`, `b.hi`).
- Loaded values: no instruction uses them.
segments.heading: `bw_new k_read`: the new read kernel

segments.text: `x0` holds the address of the buffer and `x1` its length in 8-byte words: the two arguments of `k_read` [Ref3]. The instruction computes `x1 = x0 + x1 * 8`, the address of the first byte after the buffer. It runs once per call.

Loop start. `ldp` (load pair) reads 32 bytes of the buffer at the address in `x0` into two 16-byte vector registers, `q31` and `q30`. The source writes 16 loads of 16 bytes each. gcc joined them in pairs into the 8 `ldp` of lines 26 to 33 [Ref3].

7 more `ldp` loads of 32 bytes each, at the offsets 32 to 224 bytes from `x0`. With line 26 this gives 8 loads that read bytes 0 to 255, each byte once. The data go to the 16 registers `q16` to `q31`. No instruction of the function reads these registers, and the next loop pass overwrites them.

`x0 = x0 + 256` (`0x100`). The pointer moves to the next 256 bytes.
- In the source an empty asm statement (see Words used here) stands between the 16 loads and this pointer change. The statement names the 16 loaded values as inputs. This keeps gcc from deleting the loads [Ref3].
- No instruction stands between the last load and this `add`. So the statement produced no instruction.

- `cmp` compares the end address `x1` with the pointer `x0`.
- `b.hi` jumps back to `1c64` (line 26) while the end address is higher (unsigned compare).
- No check stands before the first pass. So the loop runs at least once.
- The text after `//` is another name of the same branch condition, printed by objdump.
`ret` returns to the caller. The function saves no register, uses no stack and returns no value.

The write kernel of bw_new.
- `dup` copies the 64-bit value in `x2` into both halves of `v31`.
- The loop (`1b08` to `1b30`) writes 256 bytes per pass with 8 `stp` (store pair) instructions of 32 bytes each.
- Each thread of bw_new also calls this function for the first write to each of its buffers. This first write is not timed [Ref3].
segments.heading: `bw_new k_write` and `bw_new k_copy`: write and copy kernels of bw_new

segments.text: The copy kernel of bw_new. Per loop pass (`1ca4` to `1cf0`) 8 `ldp` read 256 bytes from the source at `x1`, and 8 `stp` write them to the destination at `x0`. The 8 loads stand before the 8 stores.

objdump text of `k_asmread` of bw_new. The loop is the text of an inline assembly block in the source. gcc added the instructions around it [Ref3].
- Loop: addresses `1b54` to `1b7c` (lines 88 to 98), 11 instructions, 44 bytes of code.
- Bytes read per loop pass: 256.
- Load instructions per loop pass: 8.
- Other instructions per loop pass: 3 (`add`, `cmp`, `b.cc`).
- Loaded values: no instruction uses them.
segments.heading: `bw_new k_asmread`: the hand-written load-only loop (asmread)

segments.text: `stp` (store pair) with `[sp, #-64]!`: first lower the stack pointer `sp` by 64 bytes, then store `d8` and `d9` there. `d8` is the low 8 bytes of vector register 8. This writes 16 bytes to the stack, not to the buffer.
`x1 = x0 + x1 * 8`: the address of the first byte after the buffer, as in line 25.

Store `d10` to `d15` to the stack, once per call. The loop overwrites the vector registers 8 to 15. AAPCS64 (the calling rules of 64-bit Arm) requires that a function leaves their low 8 bytes unchanged for its caller. So gcc saves them in lines 83 to 87 and restores them in lines 99 to 102 [Ref3].
Loop start. `ldp` reads 32 bytes of the buffer at the address in `x0` into the 16-byte registers `q0` and `q1`.

7 more `ldp` loads of 32 bytes each, at the offsets 32 to 224 bytes from `x0`. With line 88 this gives 8 loads that read bytes 0 to 255, each byte once. The data go to the registers `q0` to `q15`. No instruction of the function reads these registers, and the next loop pass overwrites them.
`x0 = x0 + 256` (`0x100`). The pointer moves to the next 256 bytes.

`cmp` compares the pointer `x0` with the end address `x1`. `b.cc` jumps back to `1b54` (line 88) while the pointer is lower (unsigned compare). This is the loop condition of lines 35 and 36 with the two operands exchanged. The loop runs at least once.

After the loop: load `d10` to `d15`, then `d8` and `d9`, back from the stack. Line 102 also raises `sp` by 64 bytes. These 4 `ldp` read 16 bytes each from the stack, not from the buffer. They run once per call.
`ret` returns to the caller. The function returns no value.
The hand-written write loop of bw_new. `dup` copies the 64-bit value in `x2` into both halves of `v0`. The loop (`1ba8` to `1bd0`) writes 256 bytes per pass with 8 `stp` of 32 bytes each.
segments.heading: `bw_new k_asmwrite` and `bw_new k_asmcopy`: hand-written write and copy loops

segments.text: The hand-written copy loop of bw_new. Per loop pass (`1bf4` to `1c40`) 8 `ldp` read 256 bytes from the source at `x1`, then 8 `stp` write them to the destination at `x0`. The function saves and restores `d8` to `d15` outside the loop, as `k_asmread` does.

objdump text of `k_read` of bw_old. gcc built it from a plain C loop that adds each 8-byte word of the buffer to one of 16 sums [Ref4].
- Loop: addresses `1b68` to `1ba4` (lines 183 to 198), 16 instructions, 64 bytes of code.
- Bytes read per loop pass: 128.
- Load instructions per loop pass: 4.
- Other instructions per loop pass: 12 (8 vector `add`, 2 integer `add`, `cmp`, `b.cc`).
- Per 256 bytes: 2 loop passes with 8 loads and 24 other instructions.
- Loaded values: each one is added to a running sum.
segments.heading: `bw_old k_read`: the old read kernel

segments.text: `movi` sets all 128 bits of the vector register `v31` to zero. `sub` lowers the stack pointer `sp` by 160 bytes (`0xa0`). The function uses this space for the 16 sums (128 bytes), a copy of the guard value of the stack protector and two saved registers.

Get the address of the guard value of the stack protector (see Words used here). `adrp` puts the page address `1f000` into `x3`. `ldr` loads the 8-byte pointer that lies 4072 bytes after this address.
Store `x29` (frame pointer) and `x30` (return address) on the stack at `sp + 144`. Then set `x29` to `sp + 144`.
Load the guard value (8 bytes) into `x4` and store a copy on the stack at `sp + 136`. Then set `x4` to zero.
4 `stp` write 4 x 32 = 128 zero bytes to the stack at `sp`. This is the array `s` of the source: the 16 sums, set to zero [Ref4]. These are stores to the stack, not to the buffer.
`cbz`: when `x1` (the buffer length in 8-byte words) is zero, jump to `1bb8` (line 203). This skips the loop.
Loop setup. `x2 = ((x1 - 1) >> 4) + 1` is the number of loop passes: one pass per 16 words (128 bytes), rounded up. `x1 = 0` is the pass counter. `movi` sets `v31` to zero again.

- Copy the zero of `v31` into `v30` to `v24`.
- The 8 registers `v24` to `v31` are the sum registers. Each one holds two 64-bit sums. Together they hold the 16 running sums.
- Lines 157 to 182 run once per call.
Loop start. `ldp` reads 32 bytes of the buffer at the address in `x0` into the 16-byte registers `q6` and `q5`.
Pass counter: `x1 = x1 + 1`.
3 more `ldp` loads of 32 bytes each, at the offsets 32, 64 and 96 bytes from `x0`. With line 183 this gives 4 loads that read bytes 0 to 127, each byte once.
`x0 = x0 + 128` (`0x80`). The pointer moves to the next 128 bytes.

8 vector adds, one per loaded register.
- `add v24.2d, v24.2d, v6.2d` takes each register as two 64-bit numbers and adds `v6` to the sum register `v24`.
- Every loaded register goes into its own sum register. So the 8 adds of one loop pass do not depend on each other.
- Each add needs the value of its sum register from the loop pass before.
`cmp` compares the pass counter `x1` with the number of passes `x2`. `b.cc` jumps back to `1b68` (line 183) while the counter is lower (unsigned compare).
After the loop: 4 `stp` store the 8 sum registers into the 128 bytes at `sp` (the array `s`). These are stores to the stack. They run once per call.

4 `ldp` load the 16 sums back from the stack, 32 bytes each, and 4 `add` start to add them up in `v31` and `v30`. Line 203 is also the target of the jump of line 170. These `ldp` read the stack, not the buffer.
Get the address of the guard value again, as in lines 159 and 160. Line 212 is a load of 8 bytes.
Two more adds of the sums into `v31` and `v30`.

- `x2` = the copy of the guard value from `sp + 136`. `x1` = the guard value now. Each of these two loads reads 8 bytes.
- `subs` subtracts `x1` from `x2` and sets the condition flags for line 221.
- `mov` sets `x1` to zero.
`add` adds `v30` to `v31`. `addp` adds the two 64-bit halves of `v31` into `d31`. `d31` now holds the total of the 16 sums.
`b.ne`: when the two guard values of lines 215 and 216 differ, jump to `1c14` (line 226).

Restore `x29` and `x30` with one 16-byte load from the stack. `fmov` copies the total into `x0`, the register that carries the return value. `add` raises `sp` by 160 bytes, and `ret` returns. The caller stores the returned total into a `volatile` variable of the thread [Ref4].
This line is reached only when the copy on the stack differs from the guard value (the compare of line 217). It calls the C library function `__stack_chk_fail`. That function ends the program.

The write kernel of bw_old. gcc built it from a plain C loop and used SVE instructions [Ref4].
- Before the loop: `cntd` puts the number of 8-byte elements of one SVE register into `x4`. `mov z31.d, x2` copies the value to write into every element of `z31`. The 3 `nop` instructions do nothing.
- Loop (`1c40` to `1c4c`): `st1d` stores the register `z31` to the buffer, `add` moves the index `x3`, `whilelo` marks the elements that are left, and `b.ne` repeats while one is left.
- A record of the same day gives 16 bytes as the default SVE register size of a process on CRB [Ref10]. With this size one loop pass writes 16 bytes.
- Each thread of bw_old also calls this function for the first write to each of its buffers. This first write is not timed [Ref4].
segments.heading: `bw_old k_write` and `bw_old k_copy`: write and copy kernels of bw_old

segments.text: The copy kernel of bw_old, also built with SVE instructions. Per loop pass (`1c70` to `1c80`) one `ld1d` loads one SVE register from the source at `x1`, and one `st1d` stores it to the destination at `x0`. With the 16-byte register size of the row above, one loop pass copies 16 bytes.

- Loaded values: no instruction uses them.

`x1 = x0 + x1 * 8`: the address of the first byte after the buffer. `x0` is the buffer address and `x1` its length in 8-byte words.
Store `d10` to `d15` to the stack. Lines 259 to 263 run once per call, before the loop.
Loop start. `ldp` reads 32 bytes of the buffer at the address in `x0` into the 16-byte registers `q0` and `q1`.

7 more `ldp` loads of 32 bytes each, at the offsets 32 to 224 bytes from `x0`. With line 264 this gives 8 loads that read bytes 0 to 255, each byte once. No instruction of the function reads the registers `q0` to `q15`, and the next loop pass overwrites them.
`x0 = x0 + 256` (`0x100`). The pointer moves to the next 256 bytes.
`cmp` compares the pointer `x0` with the end address `x1`. `b.cc` jumps back to `1c9c` (line 264) while the pointer is lower (unsigned compare). The loop runs at least once.
After the loop: load `d8` to `d15` back from the stack. Line 278 also raises `sp` by 64 bytes. These 4 `ldp` read 16 bytes each from the stack, not from the buffer. They run once per call.
`ret` returns to the caller. The function returns no value.

The hand-written write loop of bw_old. Its instructions are the same as in `bw_new k_asmwrite` (lines 107 to 120). Only the addresses differ. The loop (`1ce8` to `1d10`) writes 256 bytes per pass with 8 `stp`.

segments.text: The hand-written copy loop of bw_old. Its instructions are the same as in `bw_new k_asmcopy` (lines 124 to 153). Only the addresses differ. The loop (`1d34` to `1d80`) reads 256 bytes with 8 `ldp` and writes them with 8 `stp`.

The function `copy_barrier` of probe.o, which run_kernels.sh compiled from probe.c but never linked or ran [Ref1]. So its addresses start at 0. This candidate has the empty asm statement between the loads and the stores [Ref6]. Its instructions are the same as in `bw_new k_copy` (lines 58 to 79): 8 `ldp`, then 8 `stp`.

segments.text: The candidate without the empty asm statement [Ref6]. Loads and stores alternate here. The whole-chip test does not run this code.
The candidate without the empty asm statement and without the keyword `restrict` [Ref6]. Here the 8 `ldp` stand before the 8 `stp` again. The whole-chip test does not run this code.

The function `chase` of the binary `latency` in the folder `~/cache-perf/bench` of CRB, which run_kernels.sh did not build [Ref1].
- The loop (`1b48` to `1b70`) holds 8 `ldr x0, [x0]`. Each one loads 8 bytes from the address in `x0` into `x0`. So each load gives the address for the next load.
- The whole-chip test does not run this code.

segments.text: The function `chase` of the binary `homelat` in the same folder. Its loop (`49a4` to `49cc`) holds the same 8 `ldr x0, [x0]` loads. The whole-chip test does not run this code.

`selftest` is the self-test program. It includes the new source bandwidth.c and checks what its six kernels do to memory. Exit status 0 means that every check passed [Ref7]. Its output is in the file `selftest.txt` of the same folder.
